G43:
*If your Claim is 3,* one more letter and no seat will take you. *If it is 4,* one more and it has you. Look at any way across that costs a letter as if it were the last thing you will ever choose. If this page adds a letter, read this warning again.

*If you have been here before,* the tall passenger waits between you and Gate 0 again. Go straight to the choices.

The board clatters once, every flap at the same moment, and the Atrium goes dark.

No flicker first. The lights simply stop, and the escalators stop with them, mid-grind. In the black you can hear the glass roof ticking as it cools. Under that, from the middle of the floor, breathing, many mouths, none of them together.

The tubes stutter back, white. Wherever the tall passenger was standing a moment ago, it is somewhere else now.

Above the Atrium, the clock on the departures board has stopped. It shows the hour you have reached: count the hours ticked on your Adventure Sheet, and that is the number up there, with nothing after it but zeros. Something has been keeping your night for you.

*If you have ticked 4 hours or fewer,* you are early, and it isn't ready. It has not come as far as it meant to: it stands back by the escalator, no nearer than before, its sign only half raised, as if you have caught it dressing. Lose 1 Fear.

*If you have ticked 5 hours,* it has had all night. It stands right under the departures board, sign held high. Every lap you walked, it walked too, the long way round, practising. Somewhere in the dark it says your name, quietly, in a voice that is almost yours now. Add 1 to your Claim.

The sign is longer than it was: a column of names in different writing, each one ruled through.

*If your Claim is 3 or more,* yours is at the bottom, in capitals that lean the wrong way, nearly finished.

*If your Claim is 2 or less,* there are a few of your letters down there at most, small, with room left under them.

Dark. Light. The shoulders under the coat sit at three different heights.

Dark. Light. Among the hands holding the sign is a child's, small and careful, its knuckles white on the card.

The gaps between the flickers are getting longer. There is no rule in the Handbook for this. Gate 0 is behind it.

*If Sam is with you,* he has stopped beside you. "Rule one," he says, quietly. "It moves when they flicker. They're flickering."

If you run for Gate 0 through the flickers, and stake a letter of your name on the dark, turn to {D10}.

If you have the codeword TRUCE and Sam is with you, you can shut your eyes, hold on to him and walk blind: gain 1 Fear and turn to {G01}.

If you have the codeword CARE but not TRUCE, and Sam is with you, you can shut your eyes and walk with him, holding on loosely: gain 2 Fear and turn to {G01}.

If you have the codeword INCIDENT, you can walk past it saying the names on its sign aloud, one after another, without stopping: turn to {G01}.

If you stand still and wait for the lights to hold, turn to {G46}.

If you walk with your eyes on it the whole way, so that it cannot move but learns your face as you pass: add 1 to your Claim and turn to {G01}.
G46:
You stand still.

Dark. You hear it before the light comes back: one unhurried step, and a long coat settling.

Light. Its feet are where they were. It is nearer anyway, and the sign has tilted down so you can see the newest letters, still wet.

Dark. The breathing is in front of you now, out of time with itself. One of them catches and turns into a cough, and you know that cough.

Light. You can see the weave of the wool. Something under it presses out, round as a face, and holds there.

Dark, and it goes on. Something touches your sleeve, lightly, the way a hostess touches an elbow to guide you to your seat. Every muscle you have wants to run.

*If Sam is with you,* he has a fistful of the back of your jacket, and he doesn't make a sound.

You don't move.

Light. And it holds. One second. Two. The tubes burn white and steady, and it stands frozen in mid-lean above you.

Walk. Now, while it lasts.

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, turn to {G01}. If you fail, your nerve breaks and you back away into the dark you came from: gain 2 Fear and turn back to {G43}.
D10:
You run, and the first dark lasts a heartbeat.

When the light comes back it is nearer, and its feet haven't moved. The sign is held high.

Dark. Your trainers slap the marble. Light: nearer again. You can read your own name now, all but the end.

Dark again. Someone shouts, and it might be you.

Light. It is close enough that you see the wool of its coat pushed outwards from inside, in the shape of an open mouth.

Dark, longer this time, and close by, breathing that isn't yours.

Light. The corridor to Gate 0 is empty ahead of you, clear all the way to the lit desk. Nothing between you and the door. It isn't in front of you any more.

Behind you, close to your ear, a felt pen squeaks on card, finishing a letter. It squeaks again, and starts the next.

The lights go out, and this time they stay out.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {G43} and choose again.
G01:
The lights hold.

You are standing on new carpet. Behind you the Atrium is only an Atrium, its board turning over in the distance. Ahead is Gate 0.

It is real, and lit. Moulded seats in burnt orange. A desk in Larkvale navy. Carpet so new you can smell the glue. The clock above the desk has stopped arguing with itself and runs forward, a minute at a time, the way clocks are meant to.

The Hostess stands behind the desk, typing. She hums while she types, a song that was on every radio in the winter of 1998, and stops when she sees you. Her smile comes up a beat late, and stays.

"Good morning," she says. "Nearly."

Behind her, through the glass, the jet bridge runs out to the nose of an aircraft. At its head, where the carpet meets the open door, the tall passenger is already waiting. It got here first.

*If your Claim is 3 or more,* you can read your name on its sign from here, all but the last letters, and a space has been left for them.

*If your Claim is 2 or less,* there are a few letters at most, and a great deal of white card.

*If Sam is with you,* he sees it too. "That's not even how you spell it," he says. It is, and he knows it is. He doesn't laugh at his own joke.

If you have the codeword LOST, turn to {G26}. If you do not, turn to {G32}.
G26:
*If you have been here before,* the tall passenger stands at Gate 00 again, wearing his voice. Go straight to the choices.

The lights do not flicker.

You brace for it. All night every rule has hung on that stutter: the dark between, the shape nearer when the light returns. The strip lights over Gate 0 burn white and steady.

And the tall passenger moves.

It turns from the jet bridge and crosses the hall in full light, one long step and then another, while you watch it. It is not allowed to do this. It does it anyway. Under the coat the shoulders roll at three heights, out of step with each other.

It stops in front of a door that was blank wall a second ago. Above it, a sign: GATE 00. The front of the coat parts a little, and Sam's voice comes out.

"Don't leave me here."

It is his voice. Hoarse from a night without sleep. It comes from inside the coat and from the bridge beyond the door at once.

"Please. Not on my own."

Over the desk, the clock has stopped. Behind the desk the Hostess goes on smiling. She is crying too, without moving her face.

If you follow his voice with your eyes on the floor, turn to {G41}.

If you run straight through the door into Gate 00, turn to {D08}.

If you leave him and board without him, turn to {E_ALONE}.
G41:
You put your eyes on the carpet and keep them there.

Rule 1 says don't look at it. Rule 5 says the door you are walking towards does not exist. Both of them are shouting in your head, in the Handbook's typed capitals.

Blue, grey, blue. A coffee stain the shape of an island. A hem of grey wool slides into the edge of your sight and keeps pace with you. Breathing beside your ear, out of step with itself. Aftershave.

"Is that you?" Sam's voice, close now. "I can't see anything."

Your neck aches to lift your head.

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, turn to {G42}. If you fail, turn to {D08}.
G42:
You find a door handle where the wall should be.

You don't look up. You turn it.

It's a storage cupboard: a mop in a bucket, a shelf of paper towels, a fuse box hanging open. On the floor, knees up, earbuds in, is your brother.

He's shaking hard enough that his teeth click. Grey dust on his knuckles, fine as ash. His eyes are open and don't find you.

"Sam. Up. Now."

He weighs too much. Behind him the cupboard is getting longer. You hear the bucket slide away down a floor that wasn't there, and a hum start up in the dark at the back.

You pull. Whatever holds the other end of him lets go without interest, and the two of you go over backwards onto the carpet of Gate 0. When you look, the door is wall.

Sam stares at you. "You came back," he says. "You came back for me."

He holds on to your arm while he gets up.

Cross off the codeword LOST. Note the codeword TRUCE. Cross off 1 letter of your Claim, if you have any.

Behind you, every seat at Gate 0 creaks.

Turn to {G32}.
D08:
You run, and the door opens before you touch it. Beyond it a jet bridge runs on, bright and long and full of Sam's voice. *Don't leave me here.*

Rule 5. *Gate 00 does not exist.*

Soon your footsteps stop making a sound. Halfway, your shadow is gone. You grip the rail and see the rail through your fingers, faintly.

Sam's voice is ahead of you. It will always be ahead. It was never his. It is a sound the bridge makes, the way a shell makes the sea.

Gate 00 does not exist, and you are in it. You work out what that makes you.

Far behind you, at Gate 0, the tall passenger takes up a pen without lowering the sign, and carefully adds a letter.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {G26} and choose again.
G32:
Every seat at Gate 0 is full.

You didn't see them arrive. You never do. The Delayed sit in rows in their 1998 clothes: anoraks, shoulder pads, a shell suit with the tag still on the collar. They stand all together, with the sound of a long sigh let out.

They shuffle into a queue between you and the desk. Patient. Polite. Grey. Nobody pushes in. Nobody ever has.

Between two of them there is a gap just wide enough for a shoulder. Sam looks at the gap. "Not queuing," he says.

You go for it, shoulder first.

*If you have TRUCE,* he glances at you. "You first. You always liked a queue." He means *I'm right behind you*, and he is.

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, turn to {G02}. If you fail, turn to {G33}.
G33:
You push into the gap, and the queue closes.

No one shoves. They lean, all of them together, the way passengers lean when a train brakes, and their weight is the weight of furniture. An elbow in your ribs that won't give. A shoulder against your cheek, damp wool and old smoke. A cold hand finds yours and holds it, politely.

You can only let air out. Each time you do, the queue takes the space.

Sam's arm comes through the press, takes the collar of your jacket and hauls. You come out of the front of the line and hit the desk. Lose 3 Vigour.

Behind you the queue settles back into its line without a word of complaint. A shell-suit sleeve straightens itself.

Turn to {G02}.
G02:
*If you have been here before,* the pass is still on the desk and Sam hasn't moved. Go straight to the choices.

*Beep.*

The queue is behind you now. The Hostess passes your boarding pass under the scanner. The little light goes red, then amber, then sits there.

On the screen behind her, green letters: *LV 137. SEAT 1A.*

"Two passengers," she says. "One pass." She looks at you, then at Sam, then back at the pass, and says nothing more.

"Course," Sam says. He doesn't laugh.

The pass lies on the desk between you. Behind the glass, the tall passenger stands at the head of the bridge, sign held high.

In your jacket, the last page is folded small against your ribs. It is the only rule you haven't tried.

If you hold the pass out to Sam, turn to {G03}.

If you keep it for yourself, turn to {G04}.

If you unfold the last page and read it to the Hostess, turn to {G05}.
G03:
You hold out the pass.

Sam doesn't take it. He studies the pass, looking for the catch.

"You're serious," he says.

"Go home. Someone should be there. You were there for the rest of it."

Behind the glass, the tall passenger lowers its sign an inch, the way someone leans in to hear an answer. On the screen, *SEAT 1A* glows green.

*If you have TRUCE,* Sam folds his arms. "No. I did the rest of it on my own. I'm not doing the plane on my own as well." So you take out the last page. Turn to {G05}.

*If you do not have TRUCE,* Sam takes it before you can change your mind, and looks at you a long second: the first decent thing you've done in three years, or one more way of leaving. Turn to {E_GROUNDCREW}.
G04:
You keep it.

The Hostess nods, as if this is what everyone does in the end. "Boarding for one," she says. Above the desk the chime goes, two soft notes, and the glass door to the jet bridge slides open. Cold air comes up it, smelling of fuel and aftershave.

Sam doesn't say a word. He doesn't argue or swear or ask how you could. You could have answered any of that. He sits down in the nearest orange seat with his empty hands on his knees. He puts one earbud in, then the other, and looks at the carpet.

Home is a crematorium where you could stand at the front on your own and say Sam got delayed, and it would even be true.

At the head of the bridge, the tall passenger lowers its sign a little, politely, to let you by.

If you turn back to the desk, turn to {G02}.

If you walk on down the jet bridge without him, turn to {E_ALONE}.
G05:
You unfold the last page and read it aloud. Behind you, the queue listens.

"*Rule 8. A pass carries every name its holder loves, once every debt is settled.*"

The Hostess stops smiling. For one second her face is only a face: tired, about fifty, lipstick put on in 1998 and never taken off. When she smiles again it is properly, and a different smile altogether.

She lays the pass on the desk and taps it, once for you and once for Sam. "One pass. Two seats."

From under the desk she brings a ledger, cloth-bound and thick, and opens it at a ribbon. Your name at the top in writing you don't recognise. Sam's under it. Under both, a list.

Sam tilts his head to take it in upside down, and goes quiet at the last line.

She uncaps a pen.

Turn to {G06}.
G06:
The Hostess turns the ledger round.

*01 · REFRESHMENTS · AIRSIDE, AFTER 00:00 · OUTSTANDING IF TAKEN*

*02 · ACCOMMODATION · RM 1952 · CHECKOUT 06:00*

*03 · ANNOUNCEMENTS · OUTSTANDING IF ANSWERED*

*04 · CORRESPONDENCE · 1 MSG · 05:59 · UNHEARD*

Settle the lines in order, as she reaches them.

*If you have FED,* the kitchen door behind the desk swings open on steam, and the Chef sets down a saucer so cold it smokes. The bill says *ALL.* If you have the VOUCHER, lay it on the saucer and cross it off; he tears the bill in half. If you do not, you bring it back up, cold, onto the saucer, and then more than you ate, a peppermint in its wrapper and a child's milk tooth. He pockets the tooth. Lose 3 Vigour. Either way, cross off FED.

*If you have CHECKED IN,* a tall man with a NIGHT MANAGER badge steps out of the dark beyond the desk, and the window behind the desk shows the gate without him. "Rest well?" At *rest* he touches the ring on its chain at his collar, and offers a pen. "Don't," Sam says. A beat. "Your call." Sign your real name, and the page drinks the ink (add 1 to your Claim; remember what 4 means). Or refuse, and the hotel's cold goes through you: lose 3 Vigour. If you wear the UNIFORM, you may open your jacket on the red piping instead. "One of ours," he says, and goes. Gain 1 Fear. Whichever you choose, cross off CHECKED IN and the ROOM KEY.

She passes line 03 without stopping. There is nothing for you to do on it here: whatever you answered tonight is settled on the back page.

Her pen stops on line 04 and taps it twice. "That one's yours to settle," she says, eyes on your phone pocket. "Not at this desk."

Last, she turns to the back page.

If your Claim is now 3 or more, turn to {G44}.

Otherwise, if you have the codeword MARKED, turn to {G11}.

Otherwise, turn to {G14}.
G11:
*Ding-dong.*

The chime is close. "*Paging passenger…*" The Announcer pages Sam, slowly, the way you would page a child lost in a shop. "*We have your hand. Please make your way to Gate 00.*"

Whatever ink he carries comes up wet and black and new under his skin, gone over again from underneath. That is what the call is for. It finds him by it.

*If you have MARKED,* the old letter is in there, the one he took when he answered the first page, at your gate, and it has been waiting all night for this. Cross off MARKED.

Sam doesn't decide to move. His feet turn towards the far wall, where GATE 00 is a door again. "I can't stop," he says.

He takes a step. The carpet helps him along.

If you have the codeword TRUCE, you can hold on to him and say his name, louder than the speakers, until the ink runs off him: turn to {G14}.

If you grab Sam and drag him back, turn to {G31}.
G31:
You get both arms round him from behind and dig your heels in.

He keeps walking. He has never in his life been stronger than you, and he's dragging you across the carpet of Gate 0 like a coat he's wearing. Your shoes squeal. Your shoulders burn.

The voice pages him again, gently, an alarm on a school morning.

"Don't let go," Sam says. His face is wet. "Please don't let go."

The door to Gate 00 is ten paces away. Eight. Six.

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, turn to {G47}. If you fail, turn to {G13}.
G47:
The chime comes again, and this time it doesn't page him. It pulls.

It isn't in his legs now. It's in the ink, dragging the way the sea drags at an ankle, colder each time it goes out. His arm comes up straight, reaching for a door handle across the carpet.

You close your grip round his hand, over the black mark, and hold.

The pull goes out. It comes back weaker. After that the door to Gate 00 is plain painted wall with a fire notice on it.

Sam sits down hard and looks at his hand. The ink has gone grey, faded as an old stamp.

"That's twice tonight," he says. He doesn't say what the first time was.

Note the codeword CARE. Turn to {G14}.
G44:
The back page. Under a column of names, every one ruled through, is yours, most of it, in capitals that lean the wrong way. The last stroke is still wet.

The Hostess turns the pen round and holds it out, handle first.

*If your Claim is 4 or more,* Sam gets to the pen before you do. He draws it through your name, hard, the way you would score out a wrong answer, and the nib tears the paper. The ink won't take. It beads on your letters and runs off them, and where it ran, your name is blacker than before. He tries again, faster. At the head of the bridge the tall passenger tilts its sign so you can see the bottom of it: your name, finished but for one letter, and a space left after it exactly that size. There is too much of you on the sign for a pen to reach. Sam lays the pen down and steps back from it. Nothing is crossed off. If you have the codeword MARKED, turn to {G11}. If you do not, turn to {G14}.

*If your Claim is 3 and you have TRUCE,* Sam puts a knuckle under the first letter. "Together." You read your name aloud with him, slowly, his voice a half-beat behind yours so you don't lose your place. At the head of the bridge the sign answers. It says his name, once, the long one, in Dad's voice, the way Dad called him in from the garden. Sam's knuckle doesn't leave the page. He finishes your name first, and only then lets himself hear his. The ink lifts off in flakes. Cross off 1 letter of your Claim. If you have the codeword MARKED, turn to {G11}. If you do not, turn to {G14}.

*If your Claim is 3 and you have CARE but not TRUCE,* Sam takes her pen and strikes your name through. The ink runs back up the nib and sinks, black, under his skin. Cross off 1 letter of your Claim and turn to {G11}.

Otherwise: "Then it will take something else," she says. Turn to {G45}.
G45:
The Hostess turns to a clean page.

*If you already have FORGOT,* the voice is already gone, and she knows it. She takes the next thing instead. "The step," she says. The front step, three years ago: his one quick salute as Sam's car pulled away. She writes one word, small, and blots it. When you reach for it again, you know it happened, and you can't see it. Cross off 1 letter of your Claim, and read on from *"What did she take?"*

Otherwise: "Not the long one," she says. "The short one. The way he said it."

You hear him first. From the bottom of the stairs on a school morning. Down a bad phone line from the hospital. The lift at the start of the word, and the laugh he kept underneath it.

She writes one word, small, and blots it.

When you reach for the sound again, it isn't there. You can say the word. It is a word you have read and never heard spoken.

Cross off 1 letter of your Claim. Note the codeword FORGOT.

"What did she take?" Sam says.

"I don't know," you say, and it's true.

From the jet bridge, something says *Kite* in your father's voice, and gets it exactly right.

If you have the codeword MARKED, turn to {G11}. If you do not, turn to {G14}.
G13:
Sam slips out of your arms, and you are on your knees.

Between Sam and the door, a figure steps out of the wall: a captain's uniform, and above the collar, where the face should be, a PA speaker set into skin.

"Ladies and gentlemen," it says, in your father's voice. "We apologise for the delay."

Sam walks round it like a pillar. The grille turns to follow you instead.

It doesn't step aside. Every speaker in Gate 0 opens, and the voice comes down on you from the ceiling, the desk, the black glass: *Please remain seated.* It is Dad's voice, and your knees try to obey. *If you have FORGOT,* you don't know whose voice it is. Your knees do. Your nose bleeds into your mouth. You get a fist in its lapel, a grip on the cold steel rim of its face, your knuckles through the grille. Behind it, wet and soft, a tongue moves against them, still talking.

THE ANNOUNCER   NERVE 9   VIGOUR 12

If you win, the grille caves in, and Dad's voice stops mid-word. A step from the door, Sam stops, and turns round. Turn to {G14}.

If your Vigour reaches 0, turn to {D_VIGOUR}.
G14:
The Hostess draws a line under the last entry this desk can take, and closes the ledger.

"All debts settled," she says.

From under the counter she brings an ink stamp with a wooden handle. She presses it to the pad, then to your pass, once, twice. When she lifts it, your name is there, and under it, in the same faded purple, Sam's. Seat 0A. Beside it, as if it had always been printed there, 0B.

*If your Claim is 3 or more,* the stamp doesn't take cleanly. Sam's name comes out crisp. Yours is broken in places, and through the gaps, in black capitals that lean the wrong way, part of your name shows through from underneath, already written.

"There," she says, and her voice goes thin.

Sam takes the pass and rubs at his own name, checking it won't come off.

"Same booking," he says.

On the screen behind the desk, *1A* blinks once and goes dark. At the head of the jet bridge, the tall passenger has stopped moving at all.

If you have the codeword PROMISE, turn to {G34}. If you do not, turn to {G38}.
G34:
The phone on the gate desk rings.

Not the PA. The handset beside it: beige, curly-corded, with a real bell inside. The Hostess looks at it and doesn't pick it up. She looks at you.

You know who it is by the second ring.

You lift the receiver. No dial tone. Breathing, slow and dry: an old man who has sat in one chair for a long time and nearly forgotten how to stand. Behind it, faint, a departures board turning over. A paper bag rustles. Peppermints.

"Walter," you say.

Something on the line catches.

"I'm going to find Ruth. At arrivals. I'll tell her you tried. That you tried the whole time."

Nothing, and a sound down the line: an old man laughing, or crying. You can't tell which.

"She'll have a sign," he says, so faintly you nearly miss it. "She always made a sign."

The line clicks. The receiver is only a receiver. Lose 2 Fear.

Sam has been picking at the zip of his backpack, where the carrier bag is. He stops halfway, and leaves it.

*If you have TRUCE,* "Dad would've had his life story by the second ring," he says, "and called him Walt for the rest of it."

Turn to {G38}.
G38:
*Ding-dong.*

"*Final call,*" says the PA, and this time it is only a voice: a tired woman somewhere, reading off a screen. "*Final call for flight LV 137. All remaining passengers to Gate 0. This gate is now closing.*"

The glass door to the jet bridge slides open. Cold air comes up from the dark: fuel and rubber and night. At the far end, the aircraft door glows yellow. There is no sign of the tall passenger anywhere.

*If you have TRUCE or CARE,* Sam's hand finds yours. Neither of you looks down at it. He holds on until the speakers click off, and only then lets go.

Sam reaches the glass door first and stops there, his back to you. "Window," he says. "In case you were going to ask."

If you have the UNIFORM, turn to {G36}. If you do not, turn to {G15}.
G36:
Sam is through. As you reach the door, it slides shut between you.

A panel beside it lights red: *CREW: PLEASE USE SERVICE ACCESS.*

You look down at yourself. Navy. Red piping. LARKVALE over the heart. In the dark glass the uniform looks right on you.

On the far side, Sam waits.

Behind the desk, the Hostess watches. "Staff don't board," she says. "Staff stay. Nobody asks staff to sit by a bed, or come home. You'd never have to leave again."

The collar sits snug against your neck.

If you do not have FORGOT and you take the uniform off, cross off the UNIFORM: the panel goes dark, the door slides back, and Sam is waiting just inside. Turn to {G15}.

If you do not have FORGOT, you can instead keep it on, and never have to leave again.

If you have the codeword FORGOT, you reach for the top button, and your fingers can't remember how buttons work. It will not come off.

If the uniform stays on, Sam holds out as long as anyone could. Then the aircraft door calls him, and he goes down the bridge and in, looking back twice. Turn to {E_GROUNDCREW}.
G15:
The glass door stands open, and beyond it the jet bridge hangs out over the dark: a long, lit throat of a corridor, ribbed at the joins, sloping gently down towards the aircraft. Cold comes up it with the smell of fuel. Somewhere under your feet the whole thing creaks as it settles on its wheels, a big animal shifting its weight. The yellow of the aircraft door glows at the bottom, tiny.

You don't take the Handbook out. You learn the bridge from the threshold instead, piece by piece.

The carpet: grey-blue, worn pale down the middle.

The handrail: steel, on the right, cold enough to feel from here.

The windows: on the left, the nose of the aircraft and its open, glowing door. On the right, the dark apron and a line of blue taxiway lights.

The bend: halfway down, a ribbed rubber joint. On the panel beside it, a Larkvale poster of a mother, a father and two children waving from an aircraft window, all teeth. Next to the poster, a stretch of bare, scuffed wall.

The hum: the aircraft idling, low and steady, in your teeth.

"Carpet, rail, windows, poster, hum," Sam says.

He keeps close to the steel rail.

*If you have TRUCE,* he says it again, slower, and leaves gaps for you to fill.

If you have the TORCH and shine it down the bridge first, turn to {G37}.

If you begin walking, turn to {G16}.
G37:
You click the torch on.

The beam is yellow and heavy, and in it the bridge shows its seams. The joins between the panels run where no joins should be: one straight up through a window, one across the carpet, stopping halfway for no reason.

Where the light touches the bare wall beside the poster, the wall looks thin, like paper held up to a lamp, and a shape on the other side moves away from the light.

The torch shows things as they are, for as long as you hold it steady. Lose 1 Fear.

"And whatever that was," Sam says. "Add it to the list."

You keep the beam steady and step forward.

Turn to {G16}.
G16:
You start down the bridge, slowly.

Carpet. Rail. Windows. The bend. The hum.

You check it all again. You make yourself. The Larkvale family waving from their window. The bare scuffed wall beside them. The blue taxiway lights, in a line.

The joins tick under your feet as you cross them. Somewhere below the floor the bridge's wheels creep on the tarmac, and the whole tube settles a fraction, and stops.

Nothing is out of place. Your body wants to turn round anyway, just in case.

Sam's shoulder bumps yours. "Well?"

If you keep walking, turn to {G17}.

If you turn back, turn to {G19}.
G17:
The bridge goes on, and here it all is again.

The carpet, worn pale. The rail, cold. The windows: the aircraft's nose on the left, the blue lights on the right. The bend, and the Larkvale family waving.

And on the bare wall beside them, a brass hook. Hanging from it, a long grey wool coat.

You know the left pocket, sagging from a lifetime of keys. The darned cuff. The one odd button. The smell comes off it into the cold: aftershave and peppermints.

Sam unzips his backpack without looking. The carrier bag is there, folded small. Empty.

"I had it," he says. "I had it the whole way."

It would fit you. You could put it on, slide your arms into the sleeves, and smell him all the way to the plane.

The hum goes on, low and steady.

If you turn back and have the codeword TRUCE, turn to {G51}.

If you turn back and do not have TRUCE, turn to {G18}.

If you keep walking, turn to {G19}.
G51:
You turn to go back. Sam doesn't.

He is standing at the hook with his hand flat on the coat, over the pocket that sags from a lifetime of keys. The wool under it is warm, as a chair is when someone has only just got up.

"Give me a minute," he says.

Everything in you that has learned this bridge says go, now. Down at the bottom the yellow door won't wait for ever.

"Sam."

"I know." He doesn't move. "A minute."

He carried this coat all night in a carrier bag. He carried the man in it for longer than that. You could take his wrist and end it. Or you could stand here beside him, with every hair on your arms up, and let him be the one.

Every time the lights flicker, the bridge stretches. The bend is further off than it was a moment ago, and the yellow door further still.

If you wait with him, however long it takes, and say nothing at all until he takes his hand away by himself, gain 2 Fear and turn to {G18}.

If you lift his hand off the coat yourself, turn to {G52}.
G52:
You decide for both of you. The hum, the door, the bare wall breathing beside the poster, the bridge growing with every flicker: you have stood in it long enough.

You take his wrist and lift his hand off the sleeve.

He lets you. That is the worst of it. There is no fight in the arm at all. It comes away light, as if he had only been waiting to find out whether you would.

He zips the backpack shut over the empty carrier bag, neatly, and goes on ahead of you. He doesn't look at you for the rest of the bridge. When you say his name he says "Yeah," in his three-years-of-*fine* voice.

You took the quick way out of a room once before. He was in that one too.

Cross off the codeword TRUCE. Gain 1 Fear.

Turn to {G18}.
G18:
You turn round, and the bridge turns with you, and here it all is again.

The carpet, worn pale. The rail, cold. The windows: aircraft on the left, blue lights on the right. The bare wall at the bend. No hook. No coat. The hum, in your teeth.

The poster.

The Larkvale family is waving from their window. Mother, father, two children, arms up. Where their faces were there is smooth printed skin, the same colour as the rest of them, from hairline to chin. The waving arms are the same. The window is the same.

The smaller child's arm has come down. It is pointing at you.

Sam is staring at the bare wall, where the hook was.

If you turn back, turn to {G20}.

If you keep walking, turn to {G19}.
G19:
The bridge folds.

The carpet ripples. The rubber joint at the bend breathes in. The corridor concertinas shut around you with the sound of a heavy book closing, and there is no light at all. In the dark the hum stops, and in its place there are many mouths, none of them together.

You are at the threshold again. The open glass door. The clock behind you shows the minute it showed before. It hasn't moved, or it has gone all the way round. Gain 2 Fear.

Sam's voice is ragged. "Again," he says. "Carpet, rail, windows, poster, hum." His voice breaks on *hum*.

The bridge has one rule, and you broke it: walk past something wrong, or turn back from nothing, and it starts again.

You step through. You can't tell yet whether it is the same bridge.

Test your Fortune. If you are Lucky, it is the bridge you know: turn to {G16}. If you are Unlucky, it is a bridge you don't: turn to {G48}.
G48:
You start down the bridge again.

Carpet, worn pale down the middle. The steel rail, cold. The windows: the aircraft's nose on the left, the blue taxiway lights on the right. The bend, and the Larkvale family waving, faces and all. The bare scuffed wall beside them.

Everything is where you left it. You check twice. You count the poster's teeth.

It takes you most of the way to the bend to understand what you are listening to. Nothing. The aircraft is there in the window, door open, lit, and it makes no sound at all. Your steps are loud on the carpet. You can hear Sam swallow. You can hear the joins tick, one by one, the way you never could before.

"It's quiet," Sam whispers. "Why is it quiet?"

If you keep walking, turn to {G19}.

If you turn back, turn to {G49}.
G49:
You turn round, and the bridge turns with you.

The hum is back, low and steady, in your teeth. Carpet, worn pale. Rail, cold. Windows: aircraft on the left, blue lights on the right. The bend. The poster family, waving, every face in place. The bare wall beside it.

You look for it. You look harder than you have looked at anything tonight. The light in the windows. The pile of the carpet. How many children. Your shadow, and Sam's. There must be something, because there has always been something, and if you can't find it, it is somewhere you aren't looking.

There is nothing. The bridge is only a bridge, and it lets you look for as long as you like.

Sam's voice goes tight. "Tell me," he says. "Tell me what it is."

You can't.

If you turn back, turn to {G19}.

If you keep walking, turn to {G50}.
G50:
You keep walking. Nothing happens, and goes on not happening, all the way to the bend.

Past it, the windows on the right go black where the apron lights end, and the glass holds the two of you: two figures walking down a lit tube towards a yellow door.

Carpet. Rail. The hum.

You lift your foot, and in the window your reflection lifts its foot a half-step later. You stop. It stops, a half-step later. It isn't copying you. It is following you.

Beside it, Sam's reflection keeps perfect time with him. He hasn't noticed. He is watching the door.

You turn your head to look at it. A half-step later, it turns its head to look at you.

If you keep walking, turn to {G19}.

If you turn back, turn to {G20}.
G20:
You turn round, and there is no more bridge. There is only the door.

The aircraft doorway is close enough to touch. Yellow light spills out of it, and the smell of the cabin comes with it: stale air, coffee, and under that, flowers left too long in a hospital vase.

In the doorway, in his coat, with his face, stands Dad.

He looks well. That's what nearly takes your legs. Colour in his cheeks. Hair more dark than grey. The coat with its one odd button, done up wrong. His watch on his wrist, stopped at 05:59.

He smiles. It is exactly his smile.

Now you see the coat. Up close the grey wool is moving. Faces press out through it from inside.

A woman with a 1998 perm, flattened. A man with headphones round his neck. A boy in a school tie. An old man smelling of peppermints, his mouth shut tight. Behind them more, and behind those more, row on row, all the way down.

The face on top is Dad's. His kind brown eyes. One hand still holds the sign, lowered against the coat.

"Come and sit with me," it says, and says your full name.

*If you are his son:* "Come on, son. There's a seat by the window." *If you are his daughter:* "Come on, sweetheart. There's a seat by the window." *If neither:* "Come on, kiddo. There's a seat by the window."

Beside you, Sam makes a small sound, and sways half a step forward anyway.

If you tell him the truth, out loud, to his face, turn to {G21}.

If you attack the thing wearing your father, turn to {G22}.

If you walk straight past it into the aircraft, turn to {G23}.
G21:
You don't step forward. You don't step back. You stand in front of your father's face and say it.

*If you have TOLD,* Sam has heard the rest already, tonight. Only Dad hasn't heard it. "I didn't come," you say. "I'm sorry."

*If you do not have TOLD,* it comes out in pieces. "I didn't come." The faces stop moving. "It wasn't work. I booked a flight. March. I got to the gate." Your voice goes. "And I turned round. I was scared. Of the room. Of you, smaller. So Sam did it. All of it."

Either way, there is one word left, and you say it. "Goodbye, Dad."

The thing flinches. A ripple runs through every face in the coat, like a crowd when a door bangs. It stops leaning towards you.

If you have the codeword TOLD, Sam steps up beside you. "Bye, Dad," he says. A beat. "Your coat's done up wrong." Turn to {G24}.

If you do not have TOLD but have the codeword TRUCE, Sam is hearing this for the first time. He looks back up the bridge, and for one long second you know he could walk away up it. He looks at Dad. He stays. Turn to {G24}.

If you have neither codeword, turn to {G25}.
G25:
Sam doesn't move.

The thing with Dad's face has drawn back from that word. Nothing is stopping you now. But when you turn to Sam, his face is one you haven't seen before. It isn't angry. You could have handled angry.

"All of it," he says. "I did the tablets. I did the nights. I learned to change a bed with him in it. Every time he asked where you were, I told him you were busy."

His voice drops. "And you were scared. That's it. That's the reason."

"Sam—"

"He turned round at a gate once," Sam says. "In '98. Got right to it and came home, and never flew again, and never told us why."

"You told me not to come back."

He flinches. It's small, a jolt at the corner of his mouth, and it's real. "I know what I said. *Don't bother coming back.*" He swallows. "I stopped meaning it a long time ago. You still didn't come."

"You let me do it alone," he says.

He turns and walks back up the jet bridge, as far as the bend.

*If you have CARE,* he stops there, by the poster, and half turns. "I know what you did tonight," he says. "It doesn't cover March."

Then he is past the poster, and the glass door at the top slides open for him, and closes.

The doorway in front of you is empty. The aircraft is open, and lit.

Turn to {E_SEPARATE}.
G22:
You go for it.

For the coat: the grey wool and the faces pressed into it. Your arms sink into the cloth, and it's heavy and full, and the things inside push back against you.

A cheek. A chin. Teeth, through the wool, closing gently on your thumb. A cold grip with a wedding ring on it takes your wrist and won't let go.

Dad's face looks down at you, smiling. "Now then," it says, in the exact voice he used when you'd broken something. "Now then. That's enough."

The coat closes around your arms to the elbow. It's breathing. Behind you Sam is shouting, *don't, don't, it's still him*, and you can't tell if it's a warning or a plea.

THE PASSENGER   NERVE 10   VIGOUR 14

If you win, the coat lets go of your arms all at once, as if it has lost interest: turn to {G23}.

If your Vigour reaches 0, turn to {D_VIGOUR}.
G23:
You are through the aircraft door, and it lets you go.

No fuss. No interest. It has all the time in the world. The cabin is old, orange and brown, ashtrays in the armrests, every seat empty but two. Sam comes in behind you, shaking, his eyes on the floor.

You sit. He sits. Neither of you speaks. Nothing has been said.

In the doorway, it turns Dad's face to follow you down the aisle. The smile is perfect. The faces in the coat press so hard against the wool you can see the shape of their teeth.

"See you on the return flight," it says, kind as anything. It doesn't call you Kite.

The door closes. The plane doesn't move. You can't hear any engines. You realise you never could, and that the hum you've heard all night was never an aircraft.

Sam turns towards you and opens his mouth. Whatever he's about to say, you never hear it. The lights go out.

Turn to {E_LOOP}.
G24:
The thing in the doorway takes a step back. It has never stepped back from anything. The coat sags at the shoulders, all three heights of them, and the faces pressed into the wool begin to go under: the woman with the perm, the boy in the tie, row on row. The sign drops, names down. Dad's face stays longest. For one second it looks only tired. The wool closes over it, and the doorway is a doorway, with nothing in it but yellow light.

The aircraft is old: orange and brown fabric, ashtrays in the armrests, the Larkvale lark on every seat-back card. Just behind the first row, squeezed in where no row should fit, two reading lights are on. 0A. 0B.

*If your Claim is 4 or more,* you get as far as row 0, and no further. Seat 0A won't take you: the cushion is as hard as the desk, the belt won't reach across you, and the reading light over it goes out. A navy cuff touches your elbow, kindly, and you are walked back up the aisle and out of the door. The airport has you. Turn to {E_GROUNDCREW}.

Sam takes the window without asking. You sit beside him. The belts click.

He sits upright, his elbow tucked in, off the armrest between you.

*If you have TRUCE,* after a while he gives up on that and leans sideways until his head is on your shoulder.

He takes out one earbud and holds it up between you. You put it in. His phone is dead. The music plays anyway. It's the song Dad sang over the washing-up. The next one is his too. And the next.

"Didn't want to be on my own with it," Sam says.

Through the gap between the seats you can see row one. Seat 1A, by the window. It has been empty since 1998.

*If your Claim is 2 or less,* and you can still hear exactly how he said *Kite*, a number is waiting at the front of your mind, and nothing is in the way of it. If you know it, turn to it now.

*If your Claim is 3 or more,* the stamp on the pass in Sam's hand has smudged where your name came through. Your flight number is there, at the edge of your mind, and your name is in the way. It won't come.

If nothing comes to you, turn to {G40}.
G40:
The door thuds shut. A seatbelt sign pings on.

No crew come down the aisle. The oxygen masks stay in the ceiling, undemonstrated. The aircraft simply moves: a jolt as the tug takes it, then the slow glide back from the gate.

Past Sam's shoulder, through the oval window, Gate 0 slides away. A row of empty orange seats. An empty desk. A cleaner pushing a floor polisher past the glass. It's just a terminal at that hour, lit for no one. Your eyes sting anyway.

The engines climb from a hum to a roar. The runway lights blur. The wheels come up with a thump you feel in your stomach, and the ground lets go.

Lights of real towns slide under the wing. "We're actually going home," Sam says.

*If you have TRUCE,* "He used to time them," Sam says. "From the deck. Wheels up to cloud." He watches the wing, lips moving, counting, and doesn't tell you what he gets.

The clock on your phone says 05:59. A minute later it says 06:00.

If you have the codeword PROMISE, turn to {G39}. If you do not, turn to {E_ARRIVAL}.
G39:
Arrivals, at dawn, is a different country.

There are people here. A man with a coffee and a toddler on his shoulders. A cleaner yawning behind her trolley. Drivers at the barrier with printed name signs, bored, chatting. Pale gold light lies along a floor that shines with it.

At the end of the row, a little apart, an old woman holds a sign in felt-tip on the back of a cereal box. WALTER.

"Ruth?" you say. "He tried. The whole time."

She looks at you for a long moment, at your creased jacket and your face. "He was always late," she says. "Even for this."

She takes both your hands and holds on. "Thank you for coming to tell me."

She folds the cereal box in half, puts it under her arm, and walks out through the sliding doors into the morning. Sam stands beside you and watches her until the doors close.

Turn to {E_ARRIVAL}.
E_ARRIVAL:
Later, when people ask about the flight home, you tell them one thing.

*If you have TRUCE,* Sam gave you the window. Somewhere over the sea, in the dark, he unbuckled without a word and stood in the aisle until you understood. "Go on," he said. "You never get it." So it was your forehead against the cold plastic when the sky over the wing went from black to navy to a thin line of gold.

*If you do not have TRUCE,* Sam kept the window, and the earbud stayed between you the whole way, while the sky over the wing went from black to navy to a thin line of gold.

The plane came down through lit cloud into an ordinary morning. In the arrivals hall the board was only a board. *LV 137. LANDED.*

*If your Claim is 3 or more,* under it, for one turn of the letters, a name flickered that was nearly yours. Then it went.

The next day, at eleven o'clock, you're sitting on a low wall outside the crematorium in your good jacket, with twenty minutes to go. Sam sits down beside you, tugging at a tie he has knotted wrong. He sees what's on your screen.

*Dad. Received 05:59.* The missed call from a morning that hadn't happened yet. It has happened now. You press play, and you don't turn it away from him.

*"I should have told you both why I never…"*

"*Nothing,* you said," Sam says, watching the screen.

A breath on the line, and a cough Dad tries to hide. *"…why I never flew again. Ninety-eight. I was at the gate, and they fetched me to the desk phone, and one of you was crying down it. So I turned round. I turned round at a gate once, for you two. Don't you two turn round."*

The phone isn't against his mouth any more. It's on a table, recording the room: a monitor, a trolley, a window open on traffic. Dad, quieter, a long way off.

*If you have FORGOT,* it is his voice, all of it, until *Kite*, and then the word arrives like one you have only ever read.

*"Has Kite landed?"*

*"Yeah, Dad."* Sam's voice. *"Landed. In a taxi now."*

*"Good. That's my Kite."*

A long quiet. A chair scrapes. Sam again, close to the phone, not knowing it's there.

*"You have to make it true, or I'm a liar."*

The message ends. Sam sits with his tie in his fist, hearing himself say it to a room he thought was empty.

*If you have TRUCE,* he bumps your knee with his. It takes him two goes. "Safe landings, Kite," he says.

*If you do not have TRUCE,* he stands, straightens the tie, and waits for you. "Come on," he says. "We'll be late."
SECRET:
Seat 1A is no longer empty.

Through the gap between the headrests you can see a man by the window. Grey wool coat, buttoned wrong. Hair more dark than grey. On his wrist, a watch whose second hand, for the first time in nine days, is moving.

He turns round in his seat. His eyes are not frightened at all.

"All right, Kite," says your dad.

Beside you, Sam makes a sound like cloth tearing.

"Hiya, son," Dad says to him, more softly. "You did the hard bit. I know you did. I was there."

"Dad," you say. "Dad, I didn't—"

"I know." He reaches back between the seats and puts his hand on your head, heavy and warm, smelling of aftershave.

He looks past you, up the aisle, at the open door you came in by, for a long moment. "Turned round at a gate once," he says. "Let me do it properly this time."

You understand. A second later, so does Sam.

"Goodbye, Dad," you say. You get to say it to his face.

"Bye, Dad," says Sam.

He faces the front. His belt clicks. Out at the head of the jet bridge, the long coat opens.

They step out of it, a hundred and thirty-seven people, blinking, stretching, picking up their bags, free.

*If you have PROMISE,* Walter is among them, walking faster than any of them, towards his daughter.

Dawn comes up over the apron. Above the gate, the board flicks over.

*LV 137. PORT EVER. DEPARTED.*

Sam wipes his face on his sleeve. "I made that one up."

"I know. He kept it."

The board clicks once more. Right at the bottom, under everything that has gone, one line turns over that hasn't moved all night, and you know its year. The kiosk's till has been printing it all night, always at two minutes to midnight. Somebody else's flight. Somebody else's family, at somebody else's gate, still waiting for one of them to come back.

*LV 1987. DELAYED.*

And under it, in the small print of a till roll: *THANK YOU FOR WAITING.*
E_SEPARATE:
Sam boards last, as the door is closing.

He comes down the aisle with the pass in his hand. Level with your row he looks at the empty seat beside you, then at you, and keeps walking. "I've done worse corridors." He is past the wing and sitting near the back, at a window. He always has the window. You hear his belt click, a long way off.

You don't go back. He doesn't come forward. The seat beside you stays empty all the way home.

At dawn the plane comes down through cloud into an ordinary morning. In the baggage hall he waits at the far end of the carousel. Your aunt has booked one taxi. He sits in the front and talks to the driver about the traffic.

At the funeral he stands on the far side of the coffin. You can see him the whole time, over the lid and the lilies: tie knotted wrong, watching the photo of Dad. When the music starts, Dad's playlist, you watch him mouth the words. He doesn't look up.

Afterwards, in the car park, you have your phone out. *Dad. Received 05:59.* The missed call from a morning that hadn't happened yet, unplayed. The preview says *I should have told you both*. Both of you.

You walk over to him. "It wasn't nothing," you say. "Last night, at the gate, when you asked. It was him." You hold it out. "It's for both of us."

He looks at the screen, then at you, for a long time.

*If you have FORGOT,* you couldn't have said, now, how he said your name.

"Not today," he says.

He gets into the back of your aunt's car. There is a seat beside him.

He puts his coat on it.
E_ALONE:
Nothing stops you. The aircraft door closes behind you with a soft, final thud.

Nobody else boards. You sit by the window, which you never get, and the seat beside you stays empty the whole way.

You keep looking at it. Over the sea, in the dark. When the dawn comes up over the wing, pink and gold, you turn without thinking to say *look*, and say it to nobody.

The belt in the empty seat is buckled across the cushion. Once, over the coast, you see the cushion dip, as if a light weight has sat down. When you look properly, it's smooth.

*If you do not have LOST,* before the descent you start a text to him. *Don't bother coming back. How long did you mean it for?* You delete it.

You land. An ordinary morning. Your phone fills with messages. Your aunt: *Are you both through? Is Sam with you?* You don't answer.

In the baggage hall you look up at the arrivals board out of habit. Real cities. Landed, delayed, on time. And at the bottom, in amber, a line that shouldn't be there.

*LV 137. AWAITING 1 PASSENGER.*

At the funeral you stand at the front on your own. When people ask where Sam is, you say he got delayed. They nod. That's what happens with flights.

You will see that line again in every airport you pass through. Departures boards. Arrivals boards. A screen in a hotel lobby in a city you've moved to for work. *AWAITING 1 PASSENGER.* It never changes.

In the folder the funeral director gives you there is a bundle of hospital letters, in date order, held with a bulldog clip. The first one is dated four months before Dad called you.

And on your phone, under the funeral director's emails, Dad's voicemail is there. *Received 05:59.* The preview stops where it always stopped: *I should have told you both why I never…*

You don't play it.
E_GROUNDCREW:
The aircraft door closes, and Sam is on the other side of it.

The last you see of him is a face in a small oval window, the window seat, looking back up the bridge for you. You wave. He waves too, unsure whether you're saying goodbye or telling him to hurry. The bridge draws back from the aircraft with a long rubber sigh, and the gate is quiet.

"There," the Hostess says. "That's one home."

She comes round the desk.

*If you are not already wearing a uniform,* she has one over her arm: navy, red piping, LARKVALE over the heart, cold from a freezer, your name sewn into the collar. You put it on because she's holding it out, and because you're tired.

It fits. It always did.

She does up your cuff. "Everyone pays something at this gate," she says.

*If you held the pass out to Sam at the desk and he took it,* she adds, "You gave him the road home. Kind ones stay."

*If your Claim is exactly 3,* she adds, "You gave it your name, a letter at a time."

*If your Claim is 4 or more,* she adds, "You gave it your name, a letter at a time, until there was more of you on its sign than any seat could hold. A seat won't take a name that's spoken for."

*If you have the codeword FORGOT,* she adds, "You gave it his voice."

"They always said you were the one who left," she says. "You won't have to now."

*If you are his son:* Your badge says STEWARD. *If you are his daughter:* Your badge says STEWARDESS. *If neither:* Your badge says CREW.

She unpins her own badge and sets it on the desk. "It's Margaret," she says. "Nobody's asked in twenty-eight years." She sits in an orange seat and closes her eyes, and stops smiling.

Beyond the glass, LV 137 pushes back and turns towards the runway.

In the dark window you catch your reflection: ground staff at a gate desk, neat and kind. Your smile is right. You didn't even have to try.

Your eyes, you notice in the glass, are frightened.

They stay that way. Through the next night and the next, when the board flips to DELAYED and new passengers drift towards Gate 0 with the people they haven't spoken to in years. You smile at them. You can't make your eyes stop.

"Good evening," you hear yourself say, kind and unhurried, to a tired young man and the sister sitting apart from him. "Complimentary voucher? I'll just need your name."
E_LOOP:
In the dark, a chime. Two soft notes.

*Ding-dong.*

The board above you clatters, and every letter on it turns over.

You are sitting on hard plastic, in a row bolted to the floor. Gate 14. There's an empty seat beside you, and beyond it your brother, earbuds in, looking at nothing. Your bag is at your feet. In your pocket there's the torn stub of a boarding pass. You don't remember tearing it.

*LV 137. DELAYED.*

No new time. The clock above the desk says 11:52pm.

You know this. The cleaner with the floor polisher, gates away. The couple asleep on each other's shoulders. The one kiosk with its shutter half up.

You know it the way you know a dream the second time through, and the knowing doesn't help. At the back of your head there is a door, and a man in a grey coat saying *see you on the return flight*, and it is draining away.

Beyond the empty seat, Sam takes out one earbud.

"Typical," he says.

At the far end of the concourse, past the last gate, a tall passenger in a long coat stands without moving, holding up a handwritten sign.

This time, you can read it.

It's your name, in careful capitals. And underneath, smaller, someone has started on Sam's.

A part of you that has done this before, maybe many times, says: *this time, stay. This time, say it.*

Somewhere a door closes. Somewhere a door opens. Every gate's a door.

Cross off every codeword and item except SON, DAUGHTER or KID, clear your hours, and return your Nerve, Vigour, Fortune and Fear to their starting scores. Keep your lore. If your Claim is more than 2, set it to 2. The airport lets you start owing less.

Turn to section 1 and begin again. When it tells you the sign is too far away to read, you will know what it says.
E_FINALCALL:
*Ding-dong.*

Wherever you are, you hear it. In a corridor, at a desk, on your knees on a carpet you don't remember kneeling on. The chime is close, and kind. The hours have run out, or your name has, or your nerve. It comes to the same thing.

"*Final call,*" says the Announcer, calm and unhurried, "*for passenger…*"

And it says your name. It has had all night to practise.

It doesn't hurry. It savours. With each syllable you feel it go, the way a tooth goes: a small, bloodless gap where your name used to be fixed.

Far away, or close, someone is shouting *Kite*. You know the voice. You can't think whose it is. *Kite.* It's only a word for a toy.

*If Sam is with you,* his hand is on your sleeve, and then it isn't. He is saying your name, over and over, and it reaches you the way a voice reaches you under water.

Your feet are already walking towards the gate.

Gate 0 is lit. The Hostess doesn't ask for your pass. At the head of the jet bridge the tall passenger holds its sign high, and at last you can read all of it: a long column of names, every one ruled through, and at the bottom, fresh and finished, yours.

You're smiling. You can feel it, wide and correct, a smile for a photograph. You are more frightened than you have been in your life, and the smile doesn't move.

The coat opens for you.

It's warm inside. It smells of aftershave. There are so many people in here, pressed close, all of them frightened, all of them smiling, and you find your place among them, your face against the grey wool from the inside, looking out.

On the concourse, the board flips over. *LV 137. DELAYED.* No new time.
